question: What makes a pianissimo scamper more alarming than a loud chord?
intro: A creeping tune is interrupted by a quiet, faster scamper marked Schneller, then by a burst of sforzandi. The scamper comes twice, each time with its repeat.

sections.label: A · the creeping tune, played twice
A′ · the tune again, with the sforzandi
sections.mNote: tune returns and is broken by sf chords

sections.label: A″ · the last return and close
sections.mNote: tune returns once more and the piece ends quietly

cues.title: A tune that creeps
cues.text: Two beats to the bar, marked pp, with the pedal down. The chords carry sharps and naturals that are not in the one-sharp key signature, so the harmony shifts by small steps. The eight bars are repeated: the form analysis finds the first pass again at about 0:20.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 16 (IMSLP #03060): 2/4, one sharp, pp, Ped., accidentals in the chords, closing repeat sign after bar 8. Form analysis: 0:03–0:15 matches 0:20–0:32 (lag 17 s, mean 0.95). Report: −24.2 dB at 0:00 and G major at 0:00–0:35.

cues.title: Schneller: faster and staccato
cues.text: The word Schneller, faster, heads four bars marked pp with staccato chords over quick left-hand figures. In the recording the rate of detected attacks jumps to nearly four a second near 0:35, higher than anywhere before it.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.75 at 0:34; onsets per second rise from 2.8 at 0:30 to 3.8 at 0:35 and 3.0 at 0:40; level −13.2 dB at 0:35. Score p. 16: Schneller and pp over four bars with repeat signs.

cues.title: Sforzandi in every bar
cues.text: When the tune returns it is broken by a group of bars with an sf on most of the chords. Among the loudest windows of the recording are those at about 1:00 and 1:05, and the level drops by about eleven decibels by 1:10.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.83 at 1:02 and 0.87 at 1:10; 1:00 (−12.9 dB) and 1:05 (−12.3 dB) are among the five loudest windows (with 0:40, 1:35 and 0:35); −23.2 dB at 1:10; B minor at 1:10–1:15. Score p. 16, last system: sf chords in four successive bars.

cues.title: Liszt’s verdict
cues.text: On 24 October 1839 Liszt addressed an open letter to Berlioz in the Revue et Gazette musicale. In it he praised Schumann’s Kinderszenen and called him a poet full of feeling and a great musician. Schumann marked the passage in red in his own scrapbook of press cuttings.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue 175 Jahre Kinderszenen, item 10: Liszt’s Lettre à M. Hector Berlioz, Revue et Gazette musicale, 24 October 1839, in Schumann’s Zeitungsstimmen volume with the final paragraph marked in red; the catalogue gives the German wording “ein Dichter voll Empfindung und ein großer Musiker”.

cues.title: The scamper comes round again
cues.text: Schneller returns near 1:34. The report finds the same jump in the rate of attacks that it found near 0:35, with 3.6 onsets a second at 1:35 and 3.4 at 1:40. Listen for how little the second pass changes.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.81 at 1:34; onsets per second 3.6 at 1:35 and 3.4 at 1:40; level −13.2 dB at 1:35. Form analysis: 0:27.5–0:52 matches 1:27.5–1:52 (lag 60 s, mean 0.95). Score p. 17: Schneller, pp, repeat signs.

cues.title: The last return ends quietly
cues.text: After the second scamper the creeping tune comes back for the last time and the piece ends quietly. The report finds the sound thinning from −18 dB at 1:45 to −44 dB at 2:00, where the final chord decays.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.71 at 1:48; −17.8 dB at 1:45, −22.8 dB at 1:55, −44.4 dB at 2:00. Score p. 17, last system: the opening tune and a quiet final bar, with no ritardando printed there.

transitions.title: Faster and quieter without a pause
transitions.how: The creeping tune ends at a double bar and the next four bars are headed Schneller, faster, marked pp. The long chords of the tune give way to short staccato chords, with quick figures and a falling line in the left hand. The report still reads G major. The written dynamic drops back to pp, though the measured level in this recording rises.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.75 at 0:34; onsets 2.8 per second at 0:30, 3.8 at 0:35; G major at 0:30–0:50. Score p. 16: double bar, Schneller and pp over staccato chords with quick left-hand figures.

transitions.title: The tune returns, then breaks
transitions.to: A′ · the tune again, with the sforzandi
transitions.how: After the repeat of the scamper the creeping tune comes back at the first tempo. This time it is cut short: a few bars later the score gives most of the chords an sf, a sudden loud shock out of the pianissimo, and the tune resumes with a falling line marked ritard.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 0:50, onsets down to 2.0 per second, then novelty 0.83 at 1:02, where some of the louder windows begin. Score pp. 16–17: tune, four sf bars, then ritard.

transitions.title: Schneller a second time
transitions.from: A′ · the tune again, with the sforzandi
transitions.how: The tune ends and the four bars of Schneller begin again, once more pp, staccato and quick. The material is that of the first scamper, and it is again repeated before the tune returns.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.81 at 1:34, onsets 3.6 per second at 1:35. Form analysis matches 0:27.5–0:52 with 1:27.5–1:52. Score p. 17, third system: Schneller and pp.

transitions.title: The last return ends quietly
transitions.to: A″ · the last return and close
transitions.how: After the repeat of the second Schneller the creeping tune returns for the last time and the piece closes with it. The sforzandi do not come back, and the last bars are quiet, ending on a soft chord.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.71 at 1:48; −17.8 dB at 1:45; onsets falling from 2.6 to 1.4 per second at 1:55; −44.4 dB at 2:00. Score p. 17, last system: the opening tune and the final bar; the printed ritardando is earlier, in the middle passage.

composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
